channel.title: Deseret News - Faith
channel.description: Faith news and stories from Deseret News

item.title: 'Rejoice in Christ' -- Salt Lake Temple Celebration theme is announced
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced Tuesday that "Rejoice in Christ" will be the theme of next year's Salt Lake Temple Celebration, unveiled by President Dieter F. Uchtdorf during the first public event held in the temple's new west entrance building. The celebration, running April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027, marks the end of a seven-year renovation and will offer the general public its first chance in the temple's 134-year history to tour the pioneer-era building, with free but reservation-required tickets released starting Sept. 1 at 11 a.m. MDT via TempleSquare.org and the Temple Square app. Elder Dale G. Renlund said the celebration's new experiences are designed to help visitors "learn of Jesus Christ," and Temple Square will offer exhibitions, performances and volunteer opportunities open to anyone 16 or older, including non-members. After the open house, the temple will be rededicated and reopened for regular temple worship.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Harmer, Tad Walch

item.title: Church wins unanimous federal ruling in tithing case appeal
item.description: A unanimous three-judge panel of the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, upholding a 2025 district court dismissal of a consolidated class-action lawsuit in which nine plaintiffs sought the return of tithing donations made over roughly 25 years. Judges Harris Hartz, Gregory Phillips and Nancy Moritz found no reversible error in Judge Robert J. Shelby's ruling that the plaintiffs' fraud and misuse claims were filed after the three-year statute of limitations had expired, dismissing the case with prejudice. The panel avoided ruling directly on the broader church-autonomy doctrine that both sides had hoped to see addressed, a pattern also seen in the earlier Huntsman and Gaddy tithing cases; BYU law professor Gene Schaerr, who filed a brief on behalf of ten religious groups, called the outcome still a meaningful win for keeping courts out of churches' internal spending decisions. Church spokesman Sam Penrod reiterated that tithing funds are "carefully used and wisely managed" under church leaders' direction.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ opens doors to the Ephraim Utah Temple
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints opened the new Ephraim Utah Temple to media and invited guests Monday, ahead of a public open house running Wednesday through Sept. 19 and dedication by Elder Ronald A. Rasband of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. The temple, standing about 10 miles from the historic Manti Utah Temple, is the second in Sanpete County and was announced by President Russell M. Nelson in May 2021 after he said he received guidance to preserve the Manti temple's pioneer craftsmanship during its renovation and build a new temple in Ephraim instead. Nelson, whose mother was born in Ephraim and whose father was born in Manti, had noted at the 2022 groundbreaking that all four of his grandparents and all eight great-grandparents lived in Ephraim, immigrant converts from England, Denmark, Norway and Sweden. Utah is now home to more than 2.2 million Latter-day Saints and 32 temples that are operating, under construction, under renovation or announced.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Jane Weaver

item.title: Ground broken for Latter-day Saint temple in Coeur d'Alene, Idaho
item.description: Elder Hutch U. Fale, a General Authority Seventy of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, dedicated the site of the Coeur d'Alene Idaho Temple on Aug. 29, ahead of construction beginning on the new north Idaho temple. In his dedicatory prayer, Fale asked that the temple further the church's work, provide access to sacred ordinances for people on both sides of the veil, and stand as a symbol of peace for the surrounding Coeur d'Alene community. The brief announcement, credited to Church News, offers few additional construction details and points readers to TheChurchNews.com for the full story.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Latter-day Saint apostle dedicates Phnom Penh Cambodia Temple, where vision 'draws heavenward'
item.description: Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles dedicated the Phnom Penh Cambodia Temple on Sunday, the 222nd operating temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, telling members the building's architecture and covenants are meant to draw their gaze and hearts heavenward. Kearon noted Cambodia's history of pain from the 1970s Khmer Rouge genocide, which claimed relatives of many Cambodian Latter-day Saints, and said the temple offers a place to exchange sorrow for peace; his wife, Sister Jennifer Kearon, called the temple a gift that lets Cambodians reach the presence of God without traveling to Hong Kong or the Philippines as members previously had to. The temple, announced in 2018 by President Russell M. Nelson and broken ground in 2021, sits on a 3.2-acre site along Russian Federation Boulevard and rises about 115 feet, with membership in Cambodia having grown from a handful of converts three decades ago to more than 18,000. Phnom Penh Cambodia North Stake President Samnang Sea, who helped coordinate the open house and dedication with the Cambodian government, said the temple will make members "strong and ready to be the light of the world."
item.dc:creator: Mary Richards

item.title: 3 Utah teens represent Team USA at world ultimate championships
item.description: Three Utah teens who are members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints -- Blake Holt of Hyde Park, Silas Bell of Logan and Emilee Jensen of Bountiful -- won medals representing Team USA at the World Flying Disc Federation's World Junior Ultimate Championships in Logrono, Spain, in July. Holt, 17, took silver with the U20 men's team, while Bell, 19, and Jensen, then 18, won gold on the U20 mixed team. Jensen is returning to Spain on a mission call to Madrid, and both Holt and Bell plan to serve missions after finishing high school.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Latter-day Saint apostle shares his own struggle with overachievement
item.description: Elder Patrick Kearon of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles told a crowd of more than 15,000 at BYU's Education Week devotional that he struggles with the same overachievement he was warning against, cautioning that tying self-worth to goals and productivity can crowd out the peace Christ offers. He cited research on excessive goal-setting showing that measuring every goal can reduce the joy of achieving it, and recalled being told by the late President M. Russell Ballard to "slow down" via a video message after over-reporting on an assignment. Kearon urged listeners to protect Sabbath rest despite demanding callings -- noting apostles themselves travel 40-plus weekends a year -- and said quiet contemplation, not further striving, is how people receive Christ's peace. He told the audience their best is good enough regardless of what they accomplish.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: After controversy, artist hopes for healing at new Latter-day Saint temple
item.description: Wildlife artist Mark McKenna's landscape painting "Heart Mountain Glory" now hangs in the foyer of the Cody Wyoming Temple after a roughly two-year approval process that began with a smaller required study before the temple's Art Committee approved the full 40-by-60-inch piece. The temple itself drew local opposition over view, traffic, steeple height and lighting concerns before construction moved forward. McKenna said he hopes the painting brings peace and comfort to visitors, adding that he'd have been content seeing it hung anywhere in the temple, even a closet, as long as it was inside. The temple's public open house continues through Sept. 12, with dedication set for Oct. 25, 2026.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ expresses solidarity after deadly floods in Nepal and China
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints' Asia Area Presidency issued a statement of solidarity after flash flooding tied to a Himalayan glacier collapse killed more than 360 people and left over 1,400 missing across Nepal and Tibet as of Thursday. Elders Kelly R. Johnson, David L. Buckner and Wan-Liang Wu offered condolences on behalf of the area presidency and said the church is assessing opportunities to provide relief to affected communities and individuals. Rescue teams and military helicopters continue searching for missing people along the Nepal-China border. The statement asked for prayers for those who lost loved ones, were injured or displaced, and for communities now facing recovery and rebuilding.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: 'We weren't alone:' Spokane Latter-day Saints find faith, blessings in wildfire ashes
item.description: This companion piece to Church News' coverage of the Spokane wildfires focuses on individual members' experiences during President Dieter F. Uchtdorf and Elder Neil L. Andersen's Aug. 23 visit to the Spokane Washington North Stake. Members who lost their homes, including Andrea "Ann" Abeyta, an Eastern Shoshone woman from the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming who belongs to the stake's Seven Mile Ward, were seated near the pulpit during the special multistake meeting, and both apostles greeted them personally with handshakes as they entered. The article recounts stories from affected members about tender mercies, answered prayers and acts of service from neighbors during the fires and their aftermath, with a recurring theme that those who lost homes did not feel alone in the crisis.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: The joyful faith of Dolly Parton
item.description: Following Dolly Parton's death this week at age 80, this piece looks back at the deep Christian faith she spoke about throughout her life. Parton, whose husband Carl Dean died in March 2025 after nearly 60 years of marriage, said she believed she would see him again, and she described praying daily and doing much of her spiritual reflection between 3 and 7 a.m. She often said she talked to God "like he is my best friend" and believed in "a God light in all of us," describing her own goal as being a light and a vessel to be used. Parton requested that the hymn "If We Never Meet Again," which was sung at her father's funeral, also be sung at her own.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hess

item.title: How a national title-winning BYU coach stared down cancer with trademark grit and faith
item.description: Retired BYU Cougarettes director Jodi Maxfield, who led the dance team to 19 National Dance Alliance titles and two United Spirit Association championships over nearly 30 seasons, rang the bell marking the end of active treatment for Stage 3 ovarian cancer at the Huntsman Cancer Institute on Aug. 20. Maxfield was diagnosed in February while serving with her husband, Scott, as a Member Leader Support missionary in the England Bristol Mission. A former Cougarette herself who took over as the team's coach in 1991, she credited her family, medical team and faith, including deceased relatives, with sustaining her through treatment. Her daughter, McCall Enterline, and sister-in-law, Kelli Hintze, were among those who attended her bell-ringing ceremony.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ releases statement on regional drought and the Great Salt Lake
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints issued a statement Wednesday addressing the extended drought gripping the western United States and its effect on Utah's Great Salt Lake, which it said has reached increasingly critical low water levels in recent years. The statement follows a June 30 call from the church's Utah Area Presidency urging members to conserve water, which leaders framed as a stewardship issue rather than a political one. The church says it has donated or leased nearly 30,000 acre-feet of water to the lake since 2015 and has installed more than 3,100 smart irrigation controllers across its Intermountain West properties, saving an estimated 500 million gallons of water annually. Ongoing Temple Square renovations, including drought-tolerant landscaping and reduced turf, are expected to save up to 20 million more gallons a year once complete.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: What a tired hummingbird taught Bishop Douglas about missionaries seeking Christ
item.description: Bishop Sean Douglas, second counselor in the Presiding Bishopric, told missionaries at an Aug. 25 devotional at the Provo Missionary Training Center about a hummingbird that became trapped near a high window in his home. After trying to guide the exhausted bird outside with an extendable duster, Douglas said the hummingbird, which can die of exhaustion given how fast it must flap its wings, landed directly on the duster rather than continuing to struggle. He used the moment to teach missionaries that, in their own exhaustion, they can rely on Jesus Christ the same way, saying "you can land on Him, and He will always keep you safe." The anecdote encouraged missionaries to seek Christ's support rather than exhaust themselves alone.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ apostles minister in Spokane after devastating wildfires
item.description: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf and Elder Neil L. Andersen visited Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 23 to minister to Latter-day Saints affected by wildfires that burned about 10,000 acres, displaced 67,000 residents and destroyed or damaged roughly 900 homes and structures in early August. Within the Spokane Washington North Stake alone, 27 Latter-day Saint homes were destroyed and 12 more damaged, and more than half the stake's members were displaced. About 1,300 members gathered for a special multistake meeting at the North Stake center, with more joining by broadcast, and the apostles also toured burned neighborhoods and met individually with families who lost homes. Stake president Ronald D. Hardy said the visit reflected God's awareness of the community's suffering.
item.dc:creator: Trent Toone

item.title: Why people are handwriting the Bible
item.description: A social media trend has Christians on TikTok and Instagram handwriting the entire Bible by hand, a project participants say takes about four years at roughly 30 minutes a day given the text's 780,000-plus words and 31,000 verses. Creators like @kaylin_elise, currently transcribing Genesis in a store-bought notebook, and @j.clay, who finished all 50 chapters of Genesis using three pens, describe the practice as a way to slow down and engage more deeply with scripture. Others, including father-to-be David Sloane and a young woman known as @they.call.her.faith, are handwriting copies as personal heirlooms for a future child or spouse. The article ties the modern trend to the medieval tradition of monks hand-copying scripture in scriptoria, citing Dublin's Book of Kells as a historical touchstone.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: President Uchtdorf and Elder Andersen minister in Spokane after devastating wildfires
item.description: President Dieter F. Uchtdorf and Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles traveled to Spokane, Washington, on Sunday to comfort members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints affected by wildfires that destroyed hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands of residents in the area. The two leaders held a special multistake sacrament meeting at the North Stake center that drew about 1,300 people in person, with more joining by broadcast, and also toured burned neighborhoods. President Uchtdorf told the gathered members it was an honor to be in their presence as fellow friends in the gospel. The visit followed three separate fires that together burned thousands of acres across north Spokane in recent weeks.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Tours now underway for Guatemala's fourth Latter-day Saint temple
item.description: Public tours opened this week for the Miraflores Guatemala City Guatemala Temple, the country's fourth Latter-day Saint temple and its second in the capital, following media tours on Tuesday. The 1.5-acre temple, located in Guatemala City's Miraflores area, will be open to public tours from Aug. 27 through Sept. 12 (excluding Sundays) ahead of a dedication set for Oct. 11. Elder Patricio M. Giuffra of the Central America Area presidency called the temple a blessing that will bring the house of the Lord closer to many families, while Elder Mark D. Eddy of the Seventy said it will let members make and keep sacred covenants. Elder Gerrit W. Gong of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles also participated in temple-related events tied to the opening.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Can faith-based groups deliver humanitarian aid better? Trump is betting $2 billion they can
item.description: The Trump administration on Aug. 6 announced nearly $2 billion in U.S. foreign assistance directed toward faith-based and community organizations, including a consortium led by Compassion International and World Vision and a separate award to Samaritan's Purse, with $1.4 billion earmarked for global health services expected to reach roughly 7 million people. The shift comes after about 83% of USAID programs were terminated in 2025, and researchers interviewed for the story, including Indiana University's David King and Georgetown's Elizabeth Ferris, said faith groups bring extensive local networks of churches, mosques and clinics that can extend aid where government infrastructure has receded. Humanitarian Outcomes partner Abby Stoddard cautioned that even if funding concentrates among the largest, most capable organizations, the recipient pool would still likely be religiously and organizationally diverse. World Vision reported receiving $511 million in the last fiscal year, down from $636 million the year before, underscoring how dependent many faith-based relief groups remain on federal funding even as the funding model shifts.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: Milestones announced for first temples in Austria and American Samoa
item.description: The First Presidency of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints set new milestones for two temples that will be the first in their respective countries: the Vienna Austria Temple, announced in 2021, will break ground Oct. 17 under Elder Michael Cziesla of the Europe Central Area presidency, while the Pago Pago American Samoa Temple, announced in 2019, will be dedicated Dec. 13 by Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles. The roughly 15,300-square-foot Vienna temple will rise on a small site on Silbergasse in Vienna to serve about 4,700 members in Austria, and the Pago Pago temple will hold a public open house Nov. 4-21 and private tours Nov. 3 ahead of serving about 17,600 Latter-day Saints in American Samoa. Media are invited to preview the Pago Pago temple Nov. 2.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Use the Gospel Library app to prepare for weekly Sunday classes and meetings
item.description: Church News reported that beginning in September, Latter-day Saint wards will shift to meeting weekly for all Sunday sessions, including 25-minute Sunday School, Relief Society, elders quorum, Young Women and Aaronic Priesthood quorum meetings, and pointed members to the Gospel Library app to prepare. The app lets users swipe ahead to browse upcoming general conference talks for Relief Society and elders quorum lessons, alongside "Come, Follow Me" materials for Sunday School and "For the Strength of Youth" resources for youth classes. Church leaders emphasized that preparation by both teachers and class members at home is key to getting more out of the shortened, weekly meeting format.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: A first look inside Wyoming's newest Latter-day Saint temple
item.description: Public tours of the Cody Wyoming Temple begin Thursday, Aug. 27, and run through Sept. 12 (excluding Sundays), following media tours this week and private tours for invited guests Aug. 25-26; Elder Clark G. Gilbert of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles will dedicate the temple Oct. 25. The roughly 9,950-square-foot, single-story temple sits on a 4.69-acre site in southwestern Cody near Yellowstone National Park's eastern entrance and took about two years to build after construction began in September 2024. Its art glass and decorative paint incorporate Wyoming's state flower, the Indian paintbrush, and its interior displays original artwork including pieces titled "Heart Mountain Glory" and "Opening Day at Lower Falls." It becomes the third Latter-day Saint temple in Wyoming, joining the Star Valley and Casper temples in serving the state's nearly 67,000 church members.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: 5 steps to maintain relationships with loved ones who leave the faith
item.description: Social scientist and author Joseph W. Grenny, drawing on 40 years studying crucial conversations and his own experience with a son who left the Latter-day Saint faith, outlined a five-step approach for family members trying to preserve relationships with loved ones who leave the church. The steps begin with pausing to regulate one's own emotional reaction, since Grenny said just doing that first step well accounts for roughly 60% of a better outcome, followed by naming and examining the stories driving those feelings rather than suppressing them. He cautioned that warning signs of a struggling conversation include bearing testimony instead of asking questions or invoking eternal consequences rather than staying curious, and argued that shared, sincere understanding — not persuasion — is what ultimately keeps families connected. Grenny described the friction inherent in these relationships as part of a broader process of spiritual growth.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Construction begins on 2 new Latter-day Saint temples in the U.S. and Canada
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints held groundbreaking ceremonies Saturday, Aug. 22, for new temples in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Langford, British Columbia, near Victoria. Elder Pedro X. Larreal of the U.S. Southwest Area presidency presided over the Tulsa ceremony for the roughly 29,600-square-foot temple on a 25.7-acre site, which was first announced in 2023 and will serve nearly 54,000 Latter-day Saints in Oklahoma. Elder James E. Evanson of the Canada Area presidency presided in Langford, where an 11,400-square-foot temple announced in 2024 will rise on 4.7 acres to serve more than 211,000 church members across Canada.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Latter-day Saint leader rededicates the San Diego temple — a 'visible, tangible testimony' of the Redeemer
item.description: President D. Todd Christofferson, second counselor in the church's First Presidency, presided over Sunday's rededication of the San Diego California Temple following nearly three years of renovations that began after the building closed in July 2023. Sister Kathy Christofferson attended alongside other church leaders, and roughly 550 people took part in the rededication ceremony, more than three decades after President Gordon B. Hinckley first dedicated the temple in 1993. The 58,000-square-foot temple, perched on a ridge above Interstate 5 in La Jolla, drew about 300,000 visitors during a public open house held in June and July before the rededication, and it now serves 16 stakes across Southern California and southwestern Arizona. Christofferson told attendees the temple stands as a "testament to the faith of many generations."
item.dc:creator: Rachel Sterzer Gibson

item.title: This country now has the second-largest population of Latter-day Saints
item.description: Brazil has overtaken Mexico to become home to the second-largest population of Latter-day Saints outside the United States, with 1,573,360 members compared to Mexico's 1,572,287, the Philippines' 905,082 and the U.S.'s nearly 6.93 million. The country's membership grew by 47,924 in 2025 alone — about 12.7% of the church's global growth that year — marking a fifth consecutive year of growth since the pandemic, and Brazil now counts more than 2,000 congregations and 37 missions along with 12 operating temples and another dozen announced or under construction. Eight of the church's 110 General Authority Seventies are Brazilian, and Elder Ulisses Soares became the first Brazilian called to the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles in 2018. Church President Dallin H. Oaks has said he was eager to visit Brazil, calling it a nation he holds in high esteem.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: How youth can turn FSY's spiritual momentum into lifelong discipleship
item.description: Young Men General President Timothy L. Farnes addressed how youth can sustain the spiritual energy from For the Strength of Youth (FSY) conferences during an Aug. 11 livestream shared on Young Men Worldwide social media accounts. Farnes told youth that the change they feel isn't produced by the FSY program itself but by Jesus Christ's influence, adding that His sustaining love is available every day, not just during a conference. He pointed to the church's new Sunday youth curriculum, along with weekly activities and daily personal scripture study, as tools meant to help youth carry that momentum into lasting habits of discipleship.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Salt Lake Temple open house reservations are opening soon. Here's how to get tickets
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced that reservations for tours of the newly renovated Salt Lake Temple will open Sept. 1 at 11 a.m. MDT through TempleSquare.org and the Temple Square app, ahead of an open house and celebration running from April 5 through Oct. 1, 2027. Individual visitors may reserve up to six tickets each, while larger groups can submit separate requests, and tours will run from 8:40 a.m. to 8 p.m. Monday through Saturday and noon to 8 p.m. on Sundays. Reservations are recommended but not required for the temple tours themselves and aren't needed at all for the broader slate of exhibits, performances and other activities planned on Temple Square during the celebration. The historic temple has been closed for more than six and a half years of renovation work.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: 3 tips to prepare financially to serve a Latter-day Saint senior mission
item.description: Alek Johnson, a senior financial advisor at Peterson Wealth Advisors, laid out three steps for Latter-day Saints preparing financially for a senior mission: know the actual costs involved, put a money-management and investment plan in place well before leaving, and consolidate and organize financial records for family members. He noted the church covers travel for domestic missions and for international missions lasting more than 18 months, but missionaries are responsible for in-mission transportation, health insurance and personal expenses, while housing is covered through ward missionary funds. Johnson advised against making unfamiliar investment moves right before departing and recommended couples put together key estate documents — financial and medical powers of attorney, an advance health care directive, a trust and a will — so nothing is left unclear for their children.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Church says trademark lawsuit is about eliminating confusion caused by podcaster
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints told a federal court in Utah that its trademark lawsuit against podcaster John Dehlin and his Open Stories Foundation is not an attempt to silence criticism but to stop use of church trademarks and copyrighted images in ways that could mislead listeners into thinking Dehlin's podcast is affiliated with the church. Church attorneys argued in a filing responding to Dehlin's motion to dismiss that confusion has persisted since 2016 despite Dehlin changing his podcast's logo color and removing some copyrighted images after the church sent a warning letter in November. The church contends that disclaimers Dehlin added to his podcast descriptions are too hard for listeners to find, often buried after scrolling or behind a link. Dehlin, who filed suit in April, has said he believes his use of the church's imagery qualifies as fair use.
item.dc:creator: Tad Walch

item.title: New Missouri Historic Sites website offers resources, information for visitors
item.description: The Church History Department launched a new website devoted to Missouri's Latter-day Saint historic sites, the fourth in a series of similar state-focused sites, featuring an interactive map, articles, photos and sample itineraries for people planning visits. Curator Benedicte Caroline Dansie, who helped build the site's content, said it is meant to highlight the faith, courage and sacrifice of early church members who lived across various Missouri locations during a formative period of church history. Among the sites featured is the Liberty Jail Visitors' Center in Liberty, Missouri, which includes a full-scale replica showing the jail's original dimensions and construction.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: President Chibota speaks to missionaries of 4 sources of power
item.description: Primary General President Rosemary K. Chibota addressed missionaries at a devotional at the Provo Missionary Training Center on Tuesday, holding up a copy of the Book of Mormon as she spoke about the refining nature of missionary service. She told missionaries that the difficult moments they will face during their missions are meant to shape them into instruments the Lord can use effectively, framing hardship as purposeful rather than incidental to their service. Her remarks emphasized that the Lord is deeply invested in who missionaries become through their experience, not just in the work they accomplish.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: Is 'the right to die' an actual right?
item.description: The article examines New York's new Medical Aid in Dying Act, which took effect roughly two weeks before publication and made New York the 14th state to legalize medical aid in dying for terminally ill patients who are at least 18, mentally capable, state residents, given a six-month prognosis by two physicians, and evaluated by a mental health professional. Ethicist Alexander Raikin of the Ethics and Public Policy Center argued that death is not a right or duty but the antithesis of life, while the Cato Institute's Jeff Singer countered that a free society should let individuals remain sovereign over their own bodies. The Carmelite Sisters for the Aged and Infirm have sued over the law, saying it forces them to choose between their religious beliefs about the sanctity of life and facing fines, and the piece cites the case of Jane Allen, a Colorado woman with anorexia who was offered assisted suicide, as an example raised by critics of expanding eligibility.
item.dc:creator: Mariya Manzhos

item.title: President Christofferson will rededicate this iconic Latter-day Saint temple in California
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced that President D. Todd Christofferson, second counselor in the First Presidency, would rededicate the San Diego California Temple on Sunday, Aug. 23, with the ceremony broadcast at 11 a.m. and rebroadcast at 2 p.m. to units within the temple district. The roughly 58,000-square-foot, four-story temple had been closed since July 2023 for renovations that included new exterior finishes, landscaping, HVAC systems, roofing, art glass, carpet and lighting, following a public open house held June 18 through July 11. First announced in 1984 and originally dedicated in 1993 by Presidents Gordon B. Hinckley and Thomas S. Monson, the temple was the third built in California and now serves nearly 730,000 Latter-day Saints statewide.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz

item.title: Episode 308: Elder Bragg on family history, records custodians and the gathering of Israel
item.description: In the 308th episode of the Church News podcast, Elder Mark A. Bragg, a General Authority Seventy who serves as executive director of the church's Family History Department and FamilySearch International, discussed with reporter Mary Richards how the church partners with records custodians around the world to preserve vital records. Bragg framed that preservation work as a way of remembering God's children individually and enabling people to bring their ancestors' names to the temple, tying the effort directly to the church's broader gathering of Israel. He also spoke about the personal and emotional rewards members find in researching and expanding their family trees.
item.dc:creator: Church News

item.title: What's new and coming to Temple Square
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced new guest experiences coming to Temple Square's Joseph Smith Memorial Building, Conference Center and Salt Lake Tabernacle, designed to help visitors learn about Jesus Christ ahead of and during the Salt Lake Temple's April 5-Oct. 1, 2027 open house and celebration. The Joseph Smith Memorial Building will add a "Life of Christ Theater" with panoramic video of Christ's baptism and calming of the storm, plus interactive children's and lobby areas, alongside a chapel presentation on Sunday worship. The Conference Center, currently under renovation, will get new galleries on the church's prophets, artwork, a replica of the "Christus" statue and an interactive personal-revelation exhibit, while the historic Tabernacle will project five- to eight-minute videos of Christ's ministry onto its domed ceiling. Elder Dale G. Renlund said the additions are meant to help the millions of annual Temple Square visitors come to know the Savior better; exact opening dates will be announced later.
item.dc:creator: Amy Ortiz
